title: Judge: Cutting FEMA's Staff in Half Was Against the Rules
summary:
When a hurricane hits, who do you call? In the U.S., it's FEMA — the Federal Emergency Management Agency. It helps people before, during, and after disasters. So what happens if you try to cut its staff in half?

A federal judge says that plan was against the law. U.S. District Judge Susan Illston issued her opinion late Friday. She wrote that top Homeland Security officials late last year told FEMA's leaders to submit a staffing plan with a 50% cut — even though FEMA's own supervisors objected. "Frankly, the FEMA staffing plan number appears as if pulled from thin air," Illston wrote.

The judge said the government violated rules set up after 2005's Hurricane Katrina. Those rules put decisions about FEMA's staffing in FEMA's hands, not Homeland Security's, and stopped Homeland Security from "substantially" reducing what FEMA does.

Labor groups, including the American Federation of Government Employees, had sued. They argued the plan broke protections designed to keep FEMA independent. The lawsuit was part of a bigger push against the Trump administration's efforts to shrink the federal workforce.

Good news: the 50% cuts were never actually carried out. FEMA has even rehired some staffers who were let go. FEMA said in a statement that it is "ready for the 2026 hurricane season" and is making the agency "leaner, faster and laser-focused" on helping states and tribes.

Illston did not order a specific fix. She told both sides to meet and agree on what happens next.
why_it_matters: When a storm hits your town, the helpers who show up are part of a system with rules — and those rules are supposed to make sure the helpers are still there when families need them.

background_read: FEMA is the U.S. agency that brings help — money, supplies and workers — after hurricanes, floods and fires. It was created in the late 1970s and today it is part of the Department of Homeland Security.

Hurricane Katrina in 2005 flooded the city of New Orleans and killed many people; the slow response led to new rules meant to keep FEMA's own staffing decisions inside FEMA, not with Homeland Security.
The American Federation of Government Employees is a union — a group of workers who join together to speak up about their jobs and working conditions.
Article_Structure: WHO: U.S. District Judge Susan Illston, FEMA, Homeland Security officials, and labor groups such as the American Federation of Government Employees.
WHAT: The judge ruled that ordering FEMA's leaders to submit a plan cutting 50% of its staff was against the law.
WHERE: In a U.S. federal court; FEMA and Homeland Security are national agencies that work all over the country.
WHY: Rules created after Hurricane Katrina put FEMA's staffing decisions in FEMA's hands and stopped Homeland Security from substantially shrinking what FEMA does.

perspectives.description: They are pleased, saying the ruling protects FEMA's independence so it can keep responding quickly when disasters strike.
They argue large agencies can be slow and expensive, and that elected leaders should be able to make big changes to them.
They see this as one small piece of a much bigger fight over how much power the White House has over federal agencies.
